requirement: > `Find structural matches in available files, optionally within a file or directory. Read selected nodes separately.`
rationale:
structural: `requirements.sdk.graph.search.search_structure.mcp.description` only fixes the text of the MCP tool description: "Find structural matches in available files, optionally within a file or directory. Read selected nodes separately." It names no library, algorithm, signature, type, field or delegation interface. Any implementation that advertises that exact string behaves the same way. For example, it could come from a constant, a generated schema or a differently factored function. So no clause is structural, and no implementation evidence is needed. The supplied root, `crates/trust-but-verify/src/agent/project_sources.rs#impl[Session<'_, D>/ToolSession<D>]/fn[definitions]`, does emit the `SEARCH_STRUCTURE` definition with exactly this description. That is consistent with the requirement.

behavioral: The requirement's only observable obligation is that the published `search_structure` tool description is exactly: "Find structural matches in available files, optionally within a file or directory. Read selected nodes separately."

`crates/trust-but-verify/src/agent/project_sources.rs#mod[tests]/fn[published_tool_descriptions_match_the_contract]` covers it. It carries the `{test}` marker for this requirement. It gets the definitions from `tools.session().definitions()`. That is the same `ToolSession::definitions` method that holds the description literal. It finds the `search_structure` entry and checks it with `assert_eq!(tool.description, expected)` against the exact required string. A changed word, or a missing or extra sentence, would fail the test.

The second test, `structural_tags_select_only_the_original_enclosing_item`, also carries a `{test}` marker for the requirement. It checks behavior and parameters, not the description, so the first test is the one that matters here.

No further behavioral obligation exists.
